title: LEGO Sagrada Família (21065) gets its first reviews – biggest LEGO set yet, but not flawless
summary: Early hands-on reviews of the 12,060-piece LEGO Architecture Sagrada Família are in, praising new parts and sturdy towers but flagging accuracy issues with the Passion façade.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
Early reviews of LEGO Architecture set 21065 Sagrada Família have started appearing ahead of its official release, with New Elementary among the first to give it an in-depth look. At 12,060 pieces, it's being described as the largest LEGO set by piece count to date.

The model, designed by LEGO designer Rok Žgalin Kobe, marks 100 years since the death of architect Antoni Gaudí. Reviewers highlight a good number of new recolours and prints, including tan elements (with a drill-shaped piece used for the towers), Trans-Light Blue 6x8 plates, and printed windows reusing existing Nexo Knights shield pieces.

The build itself spans 64 bags across six separate modules, mirroring the real cathedral's actual construction sequence. Early impressions note the tower-building sections can feel repetitive, though the finished towers are said to be sturdy and look fantastic. The main criticism raised is around the lower Passion façade, which reviewers describe as quite inaccurate to the real building.

## Why it matters
As LEGO Architecture continues pushing into ultra-large, premium territory, 21065 Sagrada Família sets a new benchmark for scale and price expectations. For collectors and display builders, early reviews help gauge whether the investment of time, space and money is worth it before launch.

## What to watch next
Keep an eye out for the official LEGO reveal, full pricing and release date, plus further reviews that may expand on the Passion façade accuracy concerns.

title: LEGO used a Billund sauna to heat-test the giant Executor Super Star Destroyer
summary: Lead designer John Ho says the 136cm-long 75457 Executor was too big for LEGO's normal test oven, so it went into a public sauna in Billund instead to check for engine sagging.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
LEGO Star Wars lead designer John Ho told Brick Fanatics and other fan media that the upcoming 75457 Executor Super Star Destroyer set was too large for the company's usual heat-testing oven. At 136cm long, the model instead had to be sent to a public swimming pool sauna in Billund, Denmark, for its heat test.

According to Ho, this isn't a one-off - other large LEGO models, including the Eiffel Tower and Titanic sets, have reportedly used the same facility for testing, as it's open to the public and simply requires a peg to book time in.

The heat test is aimed at spotting potential 'sagging' in large sections such as engines, a known issue with previous oversized sets like 75367 Venator-Class Republic Attack Cruiser, where long flat sections can droop over time even without heat exposure. Ho indicated the team is also keeping an eye on how the model holds up over longer periods, not just under heat.

## Why it matters
For collectors investing in large, expensive LEGO Star Wars capital ships, structural durability matters just as much as parts count or screen accuracy. Knowing LEGO is actively stress-testing big models for sagging - even if it means using unconventional methods - should reassure buyers that display-shelf longevity is being considered during design.

## What to watch next
It'll be worth watching early owner reviews of 75457 once it's released, to see whether the sauna testing translates into a model that holds its shape better than previous oversized Star Wars sets over months of display.

title: Fan-built LEGO microscale diorama adds motorised motion to a space outpost
summary: A custom-built LEGO microscale space diorama, the 'I.E.A. Ceres Frontier Outpost', hides a motor and battery pack inside a planetary rock base to power two rotating comms towers.
bodyMarkdown:
## What happened
A LEGO fan builder has shared a new creation in their ongoing homebrew microscale space series, the Interplanetary Expedition Alliance (I.E.A.). The latest build, called the Ceres Frontier Outpost, imagines a comms station set on the dwarf planet Ceres, in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

The standout feature is motorisation. A single LEGO motor and battery pack are hidden inside the chunky planetary rock base, powering two towers: a large one that rotates a full 360 degrees, and a smaller one that pans back and forth across part of the sky. A small white tower positioned between them doubles as a switch — twisting it turns the motor on or off.

The builder notes that their usual spaceship and space station MOCs tend to be too delicate to fit motorised parts inside, so building into a solid planetary surface gave them room to hide the bulkier mechanical elements. The diorama is also packed with small scale details, including a tiny rover built using the little-known Technic Axle Nut piece as wheels.

This is a fan-made custom creation (MOC), not an official LEGO Group product.

## Why it matters
This is a great example of what's possible with LEGO microscale building and motorisation techniques, showing how hidden Power Functions-style elements can be built into terrain rather than fragile structures. It's a useful inspiration piece for builders working on space, display or stadium-style dioramas who want to add movement without compromising structural integrity.

## What to watch next
The builder says this is part of an ongoing microscale space series, so more entries in the I.E.A. universe are likely to follow — worth keeping an eye on their Instagram and future Brothers Brick features for further instalments.
